concepts.name: Prioritized functional requirements
concepts.summary: Turn a vague prompt into 'Users should be able to...' statements through clarifying questions, then keep only the top 3 core features to design for.

concepts.name: Quantified non-functional requirements
concepts.summary: State the few system qualities that matter (availability vs consistency, scale, latency, durability) tied to a part of the system and given a number, e.g. 'feed renders in < 200 ms'.

concepts.name: Estimate only when it changes a decision
concepts.summary: Skip upfront back-of-the-envelope math by default; do the numbers during the design when they decide between options, such as one instance vs sharding.

concepts.name: Delivery framework and time boxes
concepts.summary: In a 45-minute interview go requirements (~5), core entities (~2), API (~5), optional data flow, high-level design (~10-15), deep dives (~10); Alex Xu's 4 steps cover the same arc with a wrap-up.

concepts.name: Core entities and API sketch
concepts.summary: List the nouns the system stores and exchanges as a first draft, then sketch a few REST endpoints that map to the functional requirements, in minutes, not tens of minutes.

concepts.name: High-level design before deep dives
concepts.summary: First draw a simple, complete design that satisfies every endpoint, noting future complexity in a word; only then harden it against the non-functional requirements in deep dives.

concepts.name: Driving the conversation and stating trade-offs
concepts.summary: Think out loud, follow every choice with what it costs and why that fits the requirements, make a decision, and treat interviewer pushback as a hint to explore.

concepts.name: Common failure modes
concepts.summary: Candidates fail by running out of time, diving deep too early, jumping to solutions, staying silent when stuck, over-engineering, and fighting feedback.

concepts.name: The four rubric areas
concepts.summary: Interviewers assess Problem Navigation, Solution Design, Technical Excellence, and Communication and Collaboration; Problem Navigation is often the most important.

concepts.name: Mid-level vs senior expectations
concepts.summary: A mid-level candidate must deliver a complete working design with broad but shallow knowledge and drive the early steps, while the interviewer leads deep dives; a senior goes deep in ~2 areas and finds the hard problems unprompted.
